text: Six-forty, on the MTR home to Kwun Tong.
Mei can't remember what's in her fridge, so takeaway wins, again.
At home, the fridge tells the real story: a yoghurt hidden at the back,
and a second bag of spinach she didn't need.
By Friday, both go in the bin.
Hong Kong throws away about three thousand tonnes of food a day,
and two-thirds of it comes from homes like this one.
Shopping lists remember what to buy.
Food banks rescue surplus from shops.
None of them knows what's in Mei's fridge.
Meet Household Inventory.
Mei snaps her shopping, and the Sense Agent turns it into a list,
flagging anything it isn't sure about.
Nothing is saved until Mei checks it.
The app never guesses an expiry date; if the label isn't clear, it asks.
The Steward Agent keeps track of every batch, and ranks what to use first.
The Kitchen Concierge drafts dinner from what she already has:
a fifteen-minute spinach and egg skillet.
Then things change.
Ka-ho has started avoiding dairy, and the chicken was left out overnight.
The Guardrail blocks both.
It re-checks every ingredient, and no chat message can talk its way past it.
Even if an agent suggests the chicken again, the answer is: no safe meal.
The decision goes back to Mei, and she bins it.
Once Mei approves, she cooks, and only then does the app update the stock.
Two use-first items eaten, one takeaway skipped.
Every cooked or tossed tap feeds a weekly human review.
Households waste less and save money.
Community NGOs and estates reach families cheaply,
and a small subscription plus partner licences pays the bills.
No ads, no data sales.
The app keeps only the data it needs under Hong Kong's privacy law,
and a stop switch turns the AI off while the inventory stays readable.
A four-week pilot with thirty households will measure food wasted,
use-first meals and accuracy.
If people stop logging, the idea fails.
Household Inventory.
Good food. Less waste. By design.
